entry.summary: 2 minute read Ocarina of Time vs GTA VI: Switch 2 power gap 4:16 Nintendo’s remake arrives November 5, two weeks before GTA VI , on a console with under a third of the PS5’s GPU power. Design may still beat specs. Competition between major titles is becoming a theme as we move to
entry.content:
2 minute read
Ocarina of Time vs GTA VI: Switch 2 power gap
4:16

Nintendo’s remake arrives November 5, two weeks before GTA VI, on a console with under a third of the PS5’s GPU power. Design may still beat specs.

Competition between major titles is becoming a theme as we move toward the end of the year. On December 18, two massive films, Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday, hit movie theaters on the same day, in a move that the industry cannot decide is brave or borderline suicidal. The clash has already been dubbed Dunesday. And this month, two of the biggest video games of the year, Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), launch a mere two weeks apart.

 

Beyond the wild difference in content (this is more Barbenheimer than Dunesday), what makes their story particularly interesting is that they launch on hardware at opposite ends of the power scale. And it is the cheaper machine that might be the one making the stronger case for how games should be built in an industry squeezed by rising memory costs and console prices.

We’ve been here before. When Tears of the Kingdom arrived, we looked at how Nintendo turned an underpowered Switch into a platform for one of the biggest releases of all time. Now Ocarina of Time arrives on the Switch 2, which is still underpowered against the machines around it, and that still doesn’t matter.

Switch 2 by the numbers

Nintendo has not published official GPU specs for the Switch 2, but third-party analysis puts it at roughly 3.07 TFLOPS docked and 1.71 handheld, with 12 GB of LPDDR5X memory. By way of comparison, the PS5 offers 10.28 TFLOPS and 16 GB of GDDR6, while the PS5 Pro goes considerably further. In raw GPU terms, the Switch 2 has less than a third of what the base-spec PS5 brings.

That gap matters for a game such as GTA VI, which is built around a vast, dense open world that aims for photorealism. It is hard to imagine it running on Nintendo’s hardware, and Rockstar has unsurprisingly announced nothing of the kind, though it has ported games to Nintendo consoles in the past. (The most recent was Red Dead Redemption on the Switch 2 in December 2025, and Red Dead Redemption 2 is rumored to be on the way, but Rockstar has confirmed nothing.)

Nintendo plays a different game

But Nintendo designs its games around a different set of choices. With the Hyrule of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, it created a huge world and filled it with deliberately stylized graphics that eschewed photorealism for scale and interactivity.

With Ocarina of Time it’s made a different set of choices again. Previews note that Hyrule Field, which keeps the bounded layout of the 1998 original, feels small next to the Breath of the Wild map that Tears of the Kingdom reuses and expands. Whether that is a deliberate trade for polish or simply keeping true to the original, Nintendo hasn’t said (and, of course, the finished product may have a bigger play area). But the remake’s detail is where preview writers seem to be focusing their praise. We should know more soon: Metacritic has pointed to midweek for the review embargo lifting, which could mean Wednesday.

What’s in a frame?

Nintendo has not published a resolution figure for the Ocarina of Time remake, though reports based on its pre-release details list 60 fps. Digital Foundry’s analysis of the September Direct footage found gameplay at native 1080p and 60 fps, with menus at 1440p and no sign of DLSS upscaling (though it did point out some areas where it might actually have helped). That frame rate, though, is about three times that of the N64 original, which ran at roughly 20 fps.

GTA VI will be massive, no doubt about it. But Nintendo seems once more to have pulled off the trick of creating something special on a console that is comparatively feeble next to its rivals. When Tears of the Kingdom came out, we made the argument that you can chase specs as much as you like; it’s the content that really counts. And that is as true today as it was then, not to mention being as appicable to cameras as ever.

entry.title: Sony LYTIA 720: specs, availability, 4K60 HDR
entry.summary: 1 minute read Sony LYTIA 720: specs, availability, 4K60 HDR 2:48 Sony's new LYTIA 720 is a 50-megapixel stacked CMOS phone sensor with about 50% less random noise than the LYTIA 700. It supports 4K60 HDR with all-pixel autofocus. Sony's Semiconductor Solutions Corporation divisio
entry.content:
1 minute read
Sony LYTIA 720: specs, availability, 4K60 HDR
2:48

Sony's new LYTIA 720 is a 50-megapixel stacked CMOS phone sensor with about 50% less random noise than the LYTIA 700. It supports 4K60 HDR with all-pixel autofocus.

Sony's Semiconductor Solutions Corporation division has announced the LYTIA 720, an approximately 50-effective-megapixel stacked CMOS image sensor for mobile devices. It is a 1/1.56-type sensor with a 10.24 mm (0.40 in) diagonal, 1.0 μm pixels, and a Quad Bayer color filter. Basically, it inherits technologies developed for Sony's LYTIA high-end series and applies them at a lower price point.

Improved low-light performance

Ultra High Conversion Gain (UHCG) circuit technology raises charge-to-voltage conversion efficiency and reduces random noise by approximately 50% compared with the LYTIA 700. In plain English, Sony is claiming better low-light performance.

There are other gains too. Hybrid Frame-HDR (HF-HDR) combines Dual Conversion Gain-HDR (DCG-HDR), which covers low- to medium-brightness ranges in a single exposure, with a short-exposure frame for the high-brightness range. These are then merged in post-processing. Combined with UHCG, HF-HDR gives a dynamic range of 100 dB, though Sony does not say whether that figure holds in video mode. Either way, that takes us very close to 17 stops, 16.6 to be exact.

Optimized AD conversion circuits reduce conversion time and lower sensor power consumption, enabling 4K60 HDR video recording with all-pixel autofocus.

Which phones will get the LYTIA 720?

Sony names no customers and gives no pricing, so there is no confirmed phone yet that will feature the sensor. Mass-production shipping is planned for early November, though, which suggests the first devices will appear in the first half of 2027.

The 1/1.56-type format is common in mid- to upper-mid-range phones, and the LYTIA 700 it replaces has turned up in Motorola, OnePlus, and OPPO handsets. Those brands are the obvious early candidates. But it’s worth pointing out that just because the chip can perform certain tasks, it does by no means mean that the phone it sits in can as well.

We've seen a clutch of Chinese smartphones with impressive camera capabilities in recent months, including the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max and the OnePlus 16. The LYTIA 720 brings those capabilities within reach of mid-price handsets as the main sensor, though you can also expect to see it behind the telephoto camera in higher-price models.

entry.title: Sirui Swift 20mm and 40mm: specs, price, release
entry.summary: 1 minute read Sirui Swift 20mm and 40mm: specs, price, release 2:02 Sirui has launched the Swift series, kicking off with 20mm f/2.4 and 40mm f/2.2 autofocus primes for Sony E, L-mount, and Fujifilm X. Both cost $149. Sirui’s new Swift series starts with two small full-frame auto
entry.content:
1 minute read
Sirui Swift 20mm and 40mm: specs, price, release
2:02

Sirui has launched the Swift series, kicking off with 20mm f/2.4 and 40mm f/2.2 autofocus primes for Sony E, L-mount, and Fujifilm X. Both cost $149.

Sirui’s new Swift series starts with two small full-frame autofocus primes, the 20mm f/2.4 and the 40mm f/2.2, each priced at $149.

Both are available for Sony E and L-mount cameras, and for Fujifilm X, where the full-frame coverage translates to roughly 30mm and 60mm equivalents on APS-C bodies.

Swift specs, optics, and controls

The two lenses share a maximum diameter of around 69.5 mm (2.74 in), a 58 mm filter thread, and a nine-blade aperture. Length runs from 60 to 62.3 mm (2.36 to 2.45 in) and weight from 207 to 215 g (7.3 to 7.6 oz), depending on lens and mount.

Focus is driven by an STM motor, and both lenses have an AF/MF switch, a customizable Fn button, and a clicked aperture ring. And while the last is definitely in the minus column for video shooters, on the plus side Sirui pitches the pair as having low distortion and minimal focus breathing.

The 20mm f/2.4 uses 11 elements in 9 groups, including two aspherical, two ED, and two HRI elements, and focuses down to 0.2 m (7.9 in). The 40mm f/2.2 uses 11 elements in 8 groups with one aspherical and two ED elements, and focuses to 0.4 m (1.31 ft). Sirui says both are all-glass designs.

Sirui also lists both lenses as weather-sealed, with a smudge-resistant coating on the front element. Camera compatibility info is here.

The obvious rivals are Viltrox's Air series, which also offers 20mm and 40mm primes at similar price and specs. The Swift's clicked aperture ring and weather sealing seem to be the main differences.

Pricing and availability

Pre-orders are open now through Sirui's store and Amazon, with shipping from November 6.

entry.title: Dune: Part Three IMAX lenses: how Atlas built them
entry.summary: 2 minute read Dune: Part Three IMAX lenses: how Atlas built them 2:35 Atlas Lens Co. built spherical IMAX lenses for Dune: Part Three . CEO Dan Kanes explains the brief and the deadline. No spoilers, but Dune: Part Three is where it all starts to go a bit pear-shaped on Arrakis.
entry.content:
2 minute read
Dune: Part Three IMAX lenses: how Atlas built them
2:35

Atlas Lens Co. built spherical IMAX lenses for Dune: Part Three. CEO Dan Kanes explains the brief and the deadline.

No spoilers, but Dune: Part Three is where it all starts to go a bit pear-shaped on Arrakis. Based on Frank Herbert's second book in the series, Dune Messiah, it's a much darker and less optimistic tale than before, and is probably one of the least upbeat titles we can remember a major film studio releasing as its holiday season lead.

How Atlas got the call for custom IMAX lenses

All that's for another story (though we will say that if you're tempted to read the books, you should stop after the third one, Children of Dune; we wish we had). Today, we're talking lenses. Or rather, Atlas CEO and co-founder Dan Kanes is as he gives an entertaining walk-through that starts with Dune: Part Three cinematographer Linus Sandgren dropping by during prep for Wuthering Heights and asking whether Atlas could make custom lenses for the film.

“The first question that came up was, ‘How soon do you need to do this? Because it takes time to do this stuff'," says Kanes. "Maybe like nine months or so, and we’re like, ‘That’s a very short timeline, but why don’t we see?’

"In our industry, certainty is not something that we’re used to. Whether you’re a cinematographer or even if you’re in craft service, people say you don’t know you have the job for sure until the day that you show up on the film set. And in a way, that was how it was making these custom lenses with Linus and Denis and Forrest and the team for the movie. We had an idea, and we believed we were going in the right direction, and it’s just sort of about checking how far along we are on the road map, and is this still what we think we’re doing?”

What the filmmakers needed from the lenses

The initial plan was to shoot 15-perf IMAX and some form of 5-perf 65mm film. Kanes says Atlas did not want to build lenses just to say it had, so its first question was what the existing IMAX and other 65mm lenses were not doing for the filmmakers. The answer came down to full illumination of the IMAX frame without vignetting, a very specific color and style of flare to help tell the story, and lenses that could be used interchangeably across IMAX formats.

Alongside the 15-perf IMAX cameras, the production ultimately chose Panavision System 65 cameras for the 5-perf work, plus some digital cameras, so the lenses also had to give a similar look across platforms. Dune: Part Three opens worldwide on December 18.

entry.title: Adobe MAX 2026 preview: keynotes and Sneaks
entry.summary: 2 minute read Adobe MAX 2026 preview: keynotes and Sneaks 4:15 Adobe MAX returns to Miami Beach from November 10 to 12, and after a run of high-profile announcements since the summer, the video and audio tools are going to be ones to watch. Adobe MAX 2026 runs November 10 to 12 a
entry.content:
2 minute read
Adobe MAX 2026 preview: keynotes and Sneaks
4:15

Adobe MAX returns to Miami Beach from November 10 to 12, and after a run of high-profile announcements since the summer, the video and audio tools are going to be ones to watch.

Adobe MAX 2026 runs November 10 to 12 at the Miami Beach Convention Center, with pre-conference courses on November 8 and 9. The show last visited Miami Beach in 2024, before moving to Los Angeles for 2025. Happily for those unable to get there, the event also offers an online option, so remote viewers can follow the main events. Check the dedicated Adobe MAX site for details.

All times Eastern below.

Keynotes and Sneaks

The Opening Keynote is scheduled for Tuesday, November 10, from 9 to 11 am, with the Inspiration Keynote following on Wednesday from 10 to 11:30 am. Last year’s opener ran to three hours, so the shorter schedule is worth noting. Sneaks, Adobe’s extremely popular look at experimental tools that may or may not reach Creative Cloud in the fullness of time, takes place on Wednesday from 5:30 to 7 pm and is hosted this year by Terry Crews. Here’s a report on the 2025 Sneaks.

What to expect from the video tools

Adobe has been busy ahead of the show. At IBC in September, it introduced a Generative Media Tool for Premiere that fills timeline gaps with generated clips, a public beta of AI Assistant in After Effects, and a set of AI audio tools for separating sound sources and splitting overlapping dialogue. Adobe also said recently that it is bringing NVIDIA’s RTX Spark superchip to Photoshop, Premiere, and Substance 3D, which it says will deliver up to 2x faster AI processing.

There’s likely to be more announced too. Adobe always goes slightly dark between IBC and MAX while it preps some big announcements for the show. We’ll have all the stories here as they break.

Video and audio sessions to watch

The session catalog is a busy one. It’s not easy to pick highlights out, but the Video, Audio, and Motion track features a Premiere Color Mode introduction from Adobe’s Jason Druss, an audio design session for editors from film editor Vinnie Hobbs, and an After Effects motion design session from Nol Honig. The Accelerating Creativity with AI track includes a hands-on Firefly lab for building a short animation from storyboard to audio.

Speakers and sponsors

Featured speakers include Terry Crews, viral filmmaker Drex Lee, writer/director Omar S. Kamara, and YouTube storytelling strategist Hayden Hillier-Smith.

It’s not all Adobe either. Plenty of other companies get involved. Diamond sponsors are AMD, CDW, Cognizant Moment, Deloitte Digital, Google Cloud, Logitech, NVIDIA, Omnicom, and Snapdragon. Platinum sponsors include Fujifilm, HP, LucidLink, MSI, and Samsung. Fujifilm is promoting Frame.io Camera to Cloud integration on its X Series and GFX cameras.

Worth a visit…

Eddie AI is at booth 418, where it says it will show version 4 of its rough-cut editing tool, which it publicly debuted at IBC. It’s gone down well with many people, even those skeptical of AI involvement in the creative process, partly because it does so well at shouldering the donkey work from the process.

LucidLink has two sessions on Tuesday, November 10: an in-person talk at 12:45 pm ET on scaling creative production, and a virtual session at 2:30 pm ET on AI workflows.

ASUS is presenting a Creative Park talk, “Mastering Your HDR Workflow: Adobe Premiere Meets ASUS ProArt,” on Tuesday, November 10, from 3:45 to 4:15 pm ET. Adobe’s own Jason Druss will cover where HDR color workflows stand today, how Color Mode in Premiere fits into an HDR pipeline, and how display and AI-powered compute choices affect accurate results.

There are over 200 sessions and labs across seven content tracks, though, and last year the event attracted more than 150 exhibitors and over 10,000 attendees. There’s a lot to cover and likely we will be expanding this list as the show draws closer.

entry.title: Canon Q3 results, Nikon outlook: camera prices
entry.summary: 2 minute read Canon Q3 results, Nikon outlook: camera prices 3:35 Canon says camera prices may rise in 2027 if memory costs stay high. Nikon has trimmed its imaging outlook even as group profit forecasts rise. After a period of lag, while camera makers worked through memory alrea
entry.content:
2 minute read
Canon Q3 results, Nikon outlook: camera prices
3:35

Canon says camera prices may rise in 2027 if memory costs stay high. Nikon has trimmed its imaging outlook even as group profit forecasts rise.

After a period of lag, while camera makers worked through memory already secured, the memory squeeze that has already pushed up the price of cards and SSDs is showing up in earnings. The latest figures from Canon and Nikon shows it from two different angles: costs and sales.

Canon: prices may rise in 2027

On paper, all looked good for Canon in Q3. Net sales were up 4.9% to ¥1.16 trillion (about $7.3 billion), a record for the quarter. Operating profit was up 10.3% to ¥97.1 billion; net income was up 18.2% to ¥75.2 billion.

Canon said rising memory costs reduced Q3 operating profit by ¥19.8 billion, though structural reforms and a weaker yen offset them. And while the Imaging division's operating profit was up 22.7% to ¥46.8 billion, most of its sales growth came from network cameras. Interchangeable-lens camera unit sales were down 16% in Q3, and the full-year projection has been trimmed from 2.80 million to 2.75 million units, down 5% year on year.

It's not going to get any easier either, judging by the warning in the investor Q&A after the results dropped. Earlier this year Canon expected memory prices to begin easing in the second half of 2027. It no longer does. It says it has secured the memory it needs for 2026, but expects to pay more mext year, and told investors: "If these higher costs persist next year, we will absorb them through price increases."

Nikon: profit up, cameras down

On October 30, Nikon raised its full-year operating profit forecast by 50% to ¥16.5 billion and its net profit forecast by 60% to ¥16 billion. The increase comes from semiconductor equipment service revenue, US tariff refunds, and lower selling and administrative costs, including the deferral of some spending.

However, Nikon cut its full-year revenue forecast to ¥722 billion from ¥732 billion, "mainly due to" a revised second-half sales plan for Imaging Products, the division that covers cameras, lenses, and the RED and ZR cinema line. Run the numbers and the implied second-half operating profit falls to ¥7.5 billion from ¥16.5 billion. Those are our sums rather than Nikon's, and the deferred spending rather muddies the comparison. But the numbers only point one way, and it's the wrong one.

This follows an August cut to Nikon's camera target (now 850,000 units) and its Imaging revenue and profit forecasts, with weaker demand in China and memory costs cited.

Nikon has not published first-half imaging figures yet, and does not split out its cinema business, so how RED and the ZR are doing remains unclear. But the overall mood is gloomy.

Prices already heading upwards

Add recent price rises from Fujifilm and Blackmagic into the mix, plus the memory warnings Sony and Nikon have already issued, and 2027 is looking like a very good year to have bought a new camera in 2026.

Canon sells more interchangeable-lens cameras than anyone else, so its full-year results, due early next year, should show how much of the 2027 memory bill it plans to pass on, and how far the rest of the industry follows.

entry.title: Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro: specs and price
entry.summary: 1 minute read Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro: specs and price 2:10 Viltrox's new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro is $829 for Sony E and Nikon Z. It has 16 optical elements, eleven aperture blades, and voice coil autofocus. Viltrox has announced the AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens for full-frame Sony E-mount an
entry.content:
1 minute read
Viltrox AF 35mm F1.4 Pro: specs and price
2:10

Viltrox's new AF 35mm F1.4 Pro is $829 for Sony E and Nikon Z. It has 16 optical elements, eleven aperture blades, and voice coil autofocus.

Viltrox has announced the AF 35mm F1.4 Pro lens for full-frame Sony E-mount and Nikon Z-mount mirrorless cameras, joining the AF 50mm F1.4 Pro and the AF 85mm F1.4 Pro.

As the name suggests, the range is pitched at pro photographers and videographers, and this latest addition offers a wider, more flexible option than its siblings for travel and street photography. Its optical design has 16 elements in 11 groups, including 2 UA (Ultra-Precision Aspherical) elements to reduce “onion-ring” bokeh, 3 ED elements to correct axial chromatic aberration, and 4 HR elements. Eleven aperture blades produce rounded bokeh highlights. Minimum focusing distance is 0.3 m (11.8 in).

Autofocus is handled by Viltrox’s HyperVCM Focus System, driven by high-thrust voice coil motors and paired with face and eye detection. Focus breathing is minimized for video, and the lens also supports focus stacking for photography.

The lens is weather-sealed, with rubber seals to protect against dust, splashes, and moisture. It has a scratch- and wear-resistant matte black finish, and the front element has a water- and smudge-resistant coating.

The lens weighs 760 g (26.8 oz) in E-mount and 780 g (27.5 oz) in Z-mount. The E-mount version is 111 mm (4.37 in) long, while the Z-mount comes in at 112.5 mm (4.43 in) long. Both versions accept 77 mm front filters.

Pricing and availability

The AF 35mm F1.4 Pro FE and AF 35mm F1.4 Pro Z are available now at an MSRP of $829 / €859 / £739, though if you follow the links to the Viltrox store they’re currently at an impressive 20% discount, bringing them down to $663. All three in the series come in at a combined price of under $2000, which is a decent amount of lens for the money.

entry.title: COMAN T1 Mini tripod: specs and Kickstarter price
entry.summary: 2 minute read COMAN T1 Mini tripod: specs and Kickstarter price 3:02 COMAN’s T1 Mini is a 1.65 kg (3.6 lb) carbon fiber travel tripod with one-touch leg extension. It is on Kickstarter now from $279. COMAN has launched the T1 Mini, a carbon fiber travel tripod, in what is its thi
entry.content:
2 minute read
COMAN T1 Mini tripod: specs and Kickstarter price
3:02

COMAN’s T1 Mini is a 1.65 kg (3.6 lb) carbon fiber travel tripod with one-touch leg extension. It is on Kickstarter now from $279.

COMAN has launched the T1 Mini, a carbon fiber travel tripod, in what is its third crowdfunding campaign on Kickstarter. It keeps the company’s T1 one-touch height adjustment and adds a one-second Arca-Swiss quick release, three leg angles, and a modular center column.

The company says a traditional tripod takes around 15 seconds or more to set up, and that its proprietary one-touch leg-extension system cuts that to as little as 3 seconds: flip open the clamps, slide the leg sections out to the desired length, and close the clamps to lock them.

The T1 Mini weighs 1.65 kg (3.6 lb) and has a maximum payload of 6 kg (13 lb). It is built from carbon fiber, 6-series aluminum alloy, and stainless-steel hardware. The four-section legs and center column are 3K, 10-layer high-density carbon fiber. Folded length is 533 mm (21.0 in) and maximum height is 1595 mm (62.8 in). Three preset leg angles are available, and the replaceable feet come as rubber feet and steel spikes.

Modular center column

The Y-shaped center column has a concave-triangular design. The three legs nest into its grooves when folded, reducing total storage volume by 30% over the T1.

The column is modular:

  • Inverted center shaft: remove the bottom hook, pull out the center shaft, reverse it, and reinstall it for low-angle, ground-level, and macro shooting.
  • PH100 Short Center Shaft: included in the box, it replaces the standard center shaft for ultra-low-angle shooting and lets you pair the tripod with compatible fluid video heads via the 3/8"-16 mounting point.
  • PH110 Light Stand Shaft: available separately, it replaces the standard center shaft to extend height up to 2285 mm (90.0 in) and turn the tripod into a light stand or 360° camera stand.

COMAN’s Arca-Swiss quick release uses a bolt-style latch instead of a knob, and the company claims 99% compatibility with existing Arca-Swiss plates, including Peak Design-compatible plates. The panoramic ball head rotates 360° horizontally and uses a US-patented inverted-bowl design.

An optional mount attaches a smartphone to the tripod magnetically, for teleprompter use, live-view monitoring, or other applications. The tripod has two built-in ARRI-style 1/4"-20 threads at its base for accessories.

Pricing and availability

The T1 Mini is available to preorder on Kickstarter from $279 for the Black version and $299 for the Silver and Military Green versions. It is already fully funded and hopefully ships in December with a soft carrying pouch, an Arca-Swiss quick-release plate, the PH100 Short Center Shaft, a user manual, and an adjustment wrench.

entry.title: Blackmagic UltraStudio Express HD: specs and price
entry.summary: 1 minute read Blackmagic UltraStudio Express HD: specs and price 2:40 Blackmagic's UltraStudio Express HD is a USB4 capture and playback box with 3G-SDI, HDMI, and analog connections. It is available now from US$565. Blackmagic Design has announced the UltraStudio Express HD, a c
entry.content:
1 minute read
Blackmagic UltraStudio Express HD: specs and price
2:40

Blackmagic's UltraStudio Express HD is a USB4 capture and playback box with 3G-SDI, HDMI, and analog connections. It is available now from US$565.

Blackmagic Design has announced the UltraStudio Express HD, a capture and playback device for Mac, Windows, and Linux computers with USB4 or Thunderbolt 4 connections. It captures and plays back to 3G-SDI in all SD and HD video standards up to 1080p60 (525i59.94 and 625i50 in SD; 720p, 1080i, and 1080p in HD), with switching between level A and level B for 3G-SDI sources.

It also has analog YUV/NTSC/PAL video and balanced analog inputs, HDMI output for monitoring, dual SDI outputs that can switch to fill and key, a video reference input, and RS-422 remote.

“We know how important the previous UltraStudio HD Mini model has been for our customers, so we’re excited we’ve been able to rebuild it around USB4 with every broadcast connection customers need,” says Grant Petty, Blackmagic Design CEO. “That means they can keep working with the decks, switchers and monitors they’ve always had, while plugging into the computers they’re buying today or in the future. Plus, it all runs from a laptop battery, so customers can work anywhere!”

It’s competitively priced and aimed at a fairly wide range of uses. It can be used for live streaming with software such as Open Broadcaster, or to archive from old broadcast decks into standard NLE software (or the free included Media Express software). Playback via 3G-SDI works with DaVinci Resolve for broadcast editing and color correction work, or with other editing software including Final Cut Pro, Media Composer, and Premiere Pro.

Usefully for those working out in the field, video capture, playback, and power run over a single USB cable, so the unit can operate from a laptop battery. Most capture software can record to formats such as Apple ProRes, DNxHD, and 10-bit uncompressed. The unit supports uncompressed and compressed 10-bit 4:2:2 YUV or RGB.

An optional Teranex Mini Smart Panel adds front panel controls and an LCD for video preview, meters, timecode, and format information.

UltraStudio Express HD measures 140 x 170 x 44.5 mm (5.51 x 6.69 x 1.75 in) and weighs 0.61 kg (1.34 lb).

Pricing and availability

UltraStudio Express HD is available now from Blackmagic Design resellers worldwide from $565, excluding local duties and taxes.

entry.title: Insta360 Ace Pro 3: rumored specs and release date
entry.summary: 2 minute read Insta360 Ace Pro 3: rumored specs and release date 4:01 An FCC grant confirms the Insta360 Ace Pro 3 exists. Insta360 has announced nothing else, but rumors suggest a very capable performer with a 1-inch sensor and 8K video. An FCC grant for a device listed as the I
entry.content:
2 minute read
Insta360 Ace Pro 3: rumored specs and release date
4:01

An FCC grant confirms the Insta360 Ace Pro 3 exists. Insta360 has announced nothing else, but rumors suggest a very capable performer with a 1-inch sensor and 8K video.

An FCC grant for a device listed as the Insta360 Ace Pro 3 (FCC ID 2AWWH-CINSABUA) was issued to Arashi Vision, Insta360's parent company, on September 29, 2026. The model code is CINSABUA.

That means the one confirmed piece of information we have is that the camera is coming and involves dual-band WiFi (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands), plus Bluetooth. We also have a timeframe for its release, in that the manual, internal and external photos, and package label are all held confidential until March 2027 after which they then become public knowledge.

Everything else is rumor. Information is thinner than for some recent pre-release cameras (there are no package shots on X as yet), but there is enough to go on.

Likely release window

First up, we need to talk timing. As New Camera points out, recent Insta360 products have a release window that covers anything from 1 to 80 days after the FCC grant, with the Ace Pro 2 being announced just one day afterwards. Furthermore, the company has shown a definite preference for an October/November release window for the Ace series so far, which makes sense given the huge retail boost that the holiday season can provide.

Technically, that means it could be Monday.

However, the picture is complicated by what is likely to be the next-gen DJI action camera, the Osmo Action 7, which is also likely to be being prepped for release. Given the shenanigans, and that is the only word that really fits here, surrounding the two companies’ launches of their respective gimbal cameras this year, we’d imagine there is going to be a certain reactive element to all this.

Allowing for the current situation with DJI products in the US, there is going to be no matching FCC filing. But DJI leaks are typically numerous and plentiful, so there is a definite scenario where Insta360 just sits on the release date until DJI moves first.

Insta360 Ace Pro 3 specs so far

This is a summary of the speculation to date.

  • Sensor: 1-inch, 50 MP, Leica-tuned. The Ace Pro 2 uses a 1/1.3-inch sensor
  • Video: 8K30, 10-bit 4K120, and 1080p at 240 fps. A global shutter is rumored
  • Color: HDR plus a log profile
  • Stabilization: FlowState 2.0 with AI-assisted 360° horizon lock
  • Lens: around f/2.8, plus a possible dual-lens "Ultra" version with a brighter f/1.8 second lens
  • Body: a modular, rugged design with a flip touchscreen, weighing about 185 g (6.5 oz), marginally heavier than the Ace Pro 2
  • Battery: up to 200 minutes of continuous 4K recording
  • Waterproofing: 16 m (52 ft) without a case and 60 m (197 ft) with the dive case. The Ace Pro 2 is rated to 12 m (39 ft)
  • Price: Basically more than the Ace Pro 2. That launched for $399. So expect somewhere between $499 and $599, especially if that dual-lens Ultra version turns out to be real

It’s an interesting mix. A 1-inch sensor, 10-bit capture, and a log profile in a body this size would break it out of the action cam only arena and into potential B-camera territory. Certainly, the company has shown no shortage of ambition when it comes to the pro market with the Luna Pro and Luna Ultra gimbal cameras. And GoPro has rather raised the stakes with its Mission 1 series, which, despite the company’s well-publicized financial problems, has definitely moved the needle when it comes to what we expect of such devices.

Time will tell. But, if we had to pin a date on when we find out more, we would go for early November at this point.
